people.name: László Lovász
people.title: Discrete questions, richer spaces
people.bio: Lovász connected combinatorics with probability, topology, optimization and graph limits. His local lemma, theta function and topological methods became major tools.
people.impact: The theta function bridges an intractable combinatorial quantity and semidefinite optimization. It also gives a multiplicative upper bound for Shannon capacity.

sections.title: Avoid locally dependent failures
sections.text: The symmetric Local Lemma gives positive probability of avoiding all bad events if each has probability at most p and a dependency graph has degree at most d with ep(d+1)≤1. Each event must be independent of the sigma-algebra generated by its nonneighbors, not merely pairwise independent of them.

sections.title: Geometry bounds an independent set
sections.text: One formulation of theta maximizes ⟨J,X⟩ subject to tr(X)=1, X⪰0 and Xᵢⱼ=0 on edges. An independent set gives a feasible matrix, so α(G)≤ϑ(G). Multiplicativity gives an upper bound for Shannon capacity.

sections.title: Beyond one technique
sections.text: Lovász’s topological proof of Kneser’s conjecture and his work on graphons both replace a finite combinatorial problem with a richer object. Dense graphons and bounded-degree graphings are different limit frameworks.
sections.math: discrete problem → geometric or analytic representation

people.name: Leslie Valiant
people.title: Counting, circuits and learning
people.bio: Valiant introduced counting complexity, developed algebraic complexity and formulated PAC learning. He showed that changing the information requested can change a problem's complexity.
people.impact: For a zero–one bipartite adjacency matrix, the permanent counts perfect matchings. Computing it is #P-complete under polynomial-time counting reductions.

sections.title: Count instead of decide
sections.text: A #P function counts polynomial-size witnesses accepted by a polynomial-time relation. Asking whether a bipartite graph has a perfect matching is polynomial-time; counting all perfect matchings is #P-complete. This does not unconditionally separate their running times.

sections.title: Algebraic complexity
sections.text: VP consists of polynomial-degree families with polynomial-size arithmetic circuits. VNP permits an exponential Boolean summation of efficiently computed polynomials. The permanent is VNP-complete under projections over fields of characteristic different from two. In characteristic two it equals the determinant.

sections.title: Learning as a resource question
sections.text: PAC learning separates accuracy ε, failure probability δ, sample complexity and running time. A class can be statistically learnable yet computationally hard to learn under cryptographic assumptions.

people.name: Adi Shamir
people.title: Interaction reaches polynomial space
people.bio: Shamir proved IP=PSPACE, extending the algebraic interactive-proof approach of Lund, Fortnow, Karloff and Nisan. He also co-developed RSA and introduced secret sharing.
people.impact: A polynomial-time verifier can check a polynomial-space computation through randomized interaction with an unlimited prover. The theorem concerns verification, not efficient computation of the answer alone.

sections.title: Translate logic into algebra
sections.text: On Boolean inputs, negation is 1−x, conjunction is xy, and disjunction is x+y−xy. Universal quantification multiplies the two evaluations; existential quantification takes their Boolean OR. Summation alone is not existential quantification.

sections.title: Control the degree
sections.text: Repeated quantifiers can double individual degrees. Replace p by its multilinearization in x: this preserves its values at x=0 and x=1 while reducing its degree in x to one. The protocol verifies these reductions rather than writing out an exponential expression.

sections.title: The prover must speak first
sections.text: The prover sends a low-degree univariate polynomial, then the verifier samples a field point. Distinct degree-d polynomials agree at at most d points. Following a sequence of such challenges reduces a huge claim to a final directly checkable evaluation.

sections.title: What degree reduction really buys
sections.text: An exponentially large field still has polynomial-length element descriptions. The key issue is not cardinality alone: an exponentially high-degree polynomial is too long to transmit in the coefficient representation used by the protocol.
sections.math: low degree → short messages + controlled soundness

people.name: Shafi Goldwasser
people.title: Proof without disclosure
people.bio: Goldwasser co-developed probabilistic encryption and, with Micali and Rackoff, interactive proofs and zero knowledge. Her work made security a subject of precise computational definitions.
people.impact: A simulator without the secret witness must reproduce the verifier's view in the specified sense. Security against arbitrary verifiers is stronger than merely simulating an honest transcript.

sections.title: A proof is now a protocol
sections.text: Goldwasser, Micali and Rackoff introduced a model in which a randomized efficient verifier interacts with a powerful prover. Completeness guarantees honest success; soundness limits even computationally unbounded cheating provers.

sections.title: Simulation defines zero knowledge
sections.text: For every allowed cheating verifier, a simulator without the secret witness must reproduce its view in the appropriate exact, statistical or computational sense. Merely withholding the witness is not enough.

sections.title: Graph isomorphism and a subtlety
sections.text: Send a random relabeling H of one graph, then answer a challenge asking for an isomorphism from G₀ or G₁ to H. An honest-verifier transcript can be simulated by choosing the challenge first. General zero knowledge also needs a simulator handling a verifier whose challenge depends on H; the standard analysis uses rewinding.

people.name: László Babai
people.title: Symmetry becomes an algorithm
people.bio: Babai developed influential graph-isomorphism and permutation-group algorithms and helped establish Arthur–Merlin protocols. His quasipolynomial isomorphism algorithm combines combinatorial and algebraic structure.
people.impact: A large symmetry group can be represented by generators and studied through its actions. Large automorphism groups alone do not make an isomorphism instance hard.

sections.title: Search a group rather than all permutations
sections.text: Graph isomorphism asks for an adjacency-preserving bijection. Permutation groups can be represented by a small list of generators, while their orbits, stabilizers and cosets organize the candidate maps.

sections.title: Refinement and structured obstructions
sections.text: Color refinement distinguishes vertices by recursively aggregating neighborhood information. Babai’s algorithm combines more powerful combinatorial analysis with local certificates and permutation-group structure. The structural dichotomy is much more precise than “symmetric graphs are hard.”

sections.title: Two contributions to verification
sections.text: Babai introduced Arthur–Merlin games and, with Fortnow and Lund, proved MIP=NEXP. His graph-isomorphism work and his interactive-proof work connect through complexity but should not be confused as the same algorithm.

people.name: Alexander Razborov
people.title: Lower bounds and their barriers
people.bio: Razborov developed major circuit lower-bound methods. With Rudich he formulated the natural-proofs barrier, relating certain lower-bound strategies to pseudorandomness.
people.impact: If a restricted circuit admits a low-complexity approximation that the target function cannot admit, the circuit must be large. Restrictions on the circuit model are essential.

sections.title: Restrict the circuit model
sections.text: An unrestricted Boolean circuit uses AND, OR and NOT. Monotone circuits omit NOT. Razborov proved strong lower bounds in this restricted setting, including for clique, using an approximation method.

sections.title: Arithmetization for a lower bound
sections.text: Razborov–Smolensky methods approximate small constant-depth circuits with MOD-p gates by low-degree polynomials over Fₚ. Functions with incompatible modular behavior resist such approximations.

sections.title: Natural proofs
sections.text: Razborov and Rudich identified a barrier to properties that are large, efficiently recognizable from a truth table, and useful against small circuits. Under sufficiently strong pseudorandom-function assumptions, such properties would distinguish pseudorandom functions from random ones. Truth-table efficiency is exponential in the number of input variables.

people.name: Noam Nisan
people.title: Randomness for limited memory
people.bio: Nisan constructed pseudorandom generators for space-bounded computation and developed hardness-versus-randomness methods with Wigderson. He also contributed to communication complexity and algorithmic economics.
people.impact: A distribution can fool a resource-bounded observer without being truly uniform. The observer model and error parameter determine the required seed length.

sections.title: Pseudorandomness is relative
sections.text: A seed generator has support much smaller than the full random-bit space. It can still fool a bounded class of computations if their acceptance probabilities change by at most ε.

sections.title: Memory limits the observer
sections.text: An S-space computation has only exponentially many possible configurations. In the standard bounded-space model, Nisan’s generator exploits this restriction to reduce randomness dramatically; a common summary is seed length O(S log R), with the model and error conditions understood.
sections.math: limited memory → limited ability to expose correlations

sections.title: Hardness versus randomness
sections.text: With Wigderson, Nisan used carefully overlapping subsets of a seed to evaluate a hard function many times. A distinguisher can be converted into a predictor. Hardness amplification and parameter control are needed to turn worst-case hardness into a full derandomization theorem.

questions: How is space-bounded computation represented by a branching program?

people.name: Avi Wigderson
people.title: Hardness can replace randomness
people.bio: Wigderson's work connects cryptography, pseudorandomness, lower bounds and optimization. With Nisan and Impagliazzo he developed major hardness-versus-randomness results.
people.impact: The hypothesis is a sufficiently strong circuit lower bound for an efficiently describable function, not merely P≠NP. Enumerating logarithmic-length seeds then gives deterministic simulation.

sections.title: A circuit lower bound becomes an algorithm
sections.text: Nisan–Wigderson generators evaluate a hard function on overlapping portions of a seed. Small intersections let one convert a distinguisher into a small predictor. Impagliazzo–Wigderson hardness amplification supplies the bridge from suitable worst-case hardness.

sections.title: Enumerate the seeds
sections.text: A BPP algorithm using polynomially many random bits can be simulated by trying every seed when a suitable efficiently evaluable generator has O(log n) seed length. The number of seeds is then polynomial.

sections.title: A careful reverse connection
sections.text: A separate theorem of Kabanets and Impagliazzo says that sufficiently strong derandomization of arithmetic polynomial identity testing implies a major Boolean or arithmetic circuit lower bound. It should not be attributed to Wigderson, nor simplified to an unconditional arithmetic lower bound alone.
sections.math: PIT derandomization ⇒ NEXP circuit lower bound OR permanent lower bound

people.name: Richard Lipton
people.title: Small circuits, large consequences
people.bio: Lipton contributed to complexity, verification and randomized algebraic algorithms. The Karp–Lipton theorem connects small circuits for NP to a collapse of the polynomial hierarchy.
people.impact: A hypothetical small SAT circuit can be used to produce witnesses. Existentially guessing the circuit and universally checking its outputs compresses quantifier alternation.

sections.title: Nonuniform computation
sections.text: P/poly permits a separate polynomial-size circuit for each input length. There need not be an efficient algorithm that constructs those circuits. Uniform algorithms are therefore a stricter resource model.

sections.title: Use circuits to produce witnesses
sections.text: Assume SAT has small circuits. A SAT decision circuit can choose the bits of a satisfying assignment by self-reduction. For a statement ∀y∃z R(x,y,z), existentially guess such a witness-producing circuit, then universally verify R(x,y,C(y)).

sections.title: Why the argument is sound
sections.text: A false statement has some y with no witness z. No guessed circuit can output a valid witness on that y. With polynomial circuit bounds, this puts Π₂ᴾ inside Σ₂ᴾ and collapses PH. Lipton’s separate work with DeMillo helped develop randomized algebraic identity checking.

people.name: George Pólya
people.title: Probability, symmetry and discovery
people.bio: Pólya contributed to random walks, enumeration, analysis and mathematical problem solving. His recurrence theorem shows a sharp dimensional transition for lattice random walks.
people.formula: Z¹, Z² recurrent; Zᵈ transient for d≥3
people.impact: Return probabilities decay at a rate whose sum diverges in dimensions one and two. His enumeration theorem separately turns symmetry counting into cycle-index algebra.

sections.title: When a random walk returns
sections.text: For simple random walk on Zᵈ, recurrence is equivalent to divergence of the sum of return probabilities. On even times those probabilities behave like n^{−d/2}, giving recurrence exactly in dimensions one and two.

sections.title: Count modulo symmetry
sections.text: Burnside’s averaging counts orbits. Pólya’s cycle index refines it to track inventories of colors. For rotations of a square, the cycle index is (a₁⁴+a₂²+2a₄)/4; substituting every aᵢ=2 gives six binary colorings.

sections.title: Discovery is a different task
sections.text: How to Solve It emphasizes changing representations, working backward and solving simpler cases. These are heuristics for finding a proof, not inference rules that establish correctness by themselves.
sections.math: search for a proof ≠ verify a proof

people.name: Lance Fortnow
people.title: The power of separated provers
people.bio: Fortnow, with Babai and Lund, proved MIP=NEXP. He also contributed to the algebraic interactive-proof methods behind the 1990 advances in verification.
people.impact: A polynomial-time verifier can cross-check separated provers about an exponentially large claimed computation. Noncommunication constrains coordinated cheating strategies.

sections.title: Separated answers impose consistency
sections.text: Multiple provers may coordinate before the protocol but cannot communicate during it. The verifier can send related questions whose connection is hidden from either prover. Their answers must agree with a common global account.

sections.title: Why exponential time appears
sections.text: An NEXP computation can have an exponentially large witness. The BFL theorem encodes such a witness so that a polynomial-time verifier can perform algebraic and consistency checks without reading the whole object.

sections.title: A path toward approximation
sections.text: A nonadaptive local verifier can be converted into a constraint system with one constraint for each random string. Its completeness–soundness gap becomes an optimization gap. Deriving the full PCP theorem requires additional results; it is not immediate from the equality alone.

people.name: Thomas Vidick
people.title: Quantum correlations and verification
people.bio: Vidick works on quantum information and complexity. With Ji, Natarajan, Wright and Yuen, he proved MIP*=RE, connecting entangled provers with undecidability.
people.impact: The verifier is classical, while the provers may share entanglement of unbounded finite dimension. The equality does not give an ordinary algorithm for deciding the halting problem.

sections.title: The communication rule does not change
sections.text: Entangled provers remain unable to communicate during the protocol. They may share a state and answer by local measurements, producing correlations not available to classical shared randomness.

sections.title: A surprising complexity equality
sections.text: Ji, Natarajan, Vidick, Wright and Yuen proved that finite-dimensional entangled multiprover verification with a completeness–soundness gap captures recursively enumerable languages. The allowed finite dimension is not bounded in advance by a computable function of the input.

sections.title: Do not confuse verification with decision
sections.text: The verifier alone does not decide membership. Finding or bounding the necessary prover strategy is the source of noncomputability. The result also has consequences for operator-algebra problems.
sections.math: classical verifier + entangled strategies ≠ a halting decider

people.name: Johan Håstad
people.title: The sharp edge of approximation
people.bio: Håstad proved landmark circuit lower bounds and optimal inapproximability results. His PCP constructions exposed quantitative limits on efficient approximation.
people.impact: For clauses with three distinct variables, a random assignment satisfies each with probability 7/8. Beating the corresponding approximation threshold is NP-hard, up to any fixed positive slack.

sections.title: Why 7/8 appears
sections.text: An OR of three distinct noncontradictory literals is false on exactly one of eight assignments. A uniformly random assignment therefore satisfies 7m/8 clauses in expectation, and conditional expectations can remove the randomness.

sections.title: A constant gap is the key
sections.text: Ordinary NP-hardness may separate full satisfaction from failure on one clause out of millions. Approximation hardness requires a robust gap. Håstad constructed PCPs giving essentially optimal gaps for MAX-E3SAT and MAX-E3LIN.
sections.math: near 1 versus near 7/8; near 1 versus near 1/2

sections.text: Long-code tests encode a label i as the dictator f(x)=xᵢ. Fourier analysis shows how unusually high acceptance reveals coordinates usable as labels. The test and predicate determine the quantitative hardness.

people.name: Subhash Khot
people.title: A conjecture that reorganized a field
people.bio: Khot introduced the Unique Games Conjecture. Its consequences link approximation thresholds with Fourier analysis, Gaussian geometry and semidefinite programming.
people.impact: A permutation constraint determines one label from the other. The conjecture concerns distinguishing nearly satisfiable systems from systems of very low optimum, not exact satisfiability.

sections.title: The constraint is uniquely satisfiable in one direction
sections.text: Every edge carries a permutation π, requiring xᵥ=π(xᵤ). Once one endpoint label is chosen, the other is forced. Exact full satisfiability can be tested by propagation; the conjecture concerns robust approximation gaps.

sections.title: State the hypothesis carefully
sections.text: The Unique Games Conjecture posits NP-hardness of distinguishing optimum at least 1−ε from optimum at most δ, for every fixed positive ε and δ with a sufficiently large fixed alphabet. Consequences below are conditional on this conjecture, not unconditional hardness theorems.

sections.title: Algorithms and hardness meet
sections.text: Khot, Kindler, Mossel and O’Donnell related MAX-CUT hardness to noise stability. Conditional on UGC, beating the Goemans–Williamson ratio by a fixed amount would be NP-hard. Raghavendra extended the relationship to a general fixed-CSP framework.
sections.math: UGC ⇒ the MAX-CUT threshold is αGW

people.name: Ryan O’Donnell
people.title: Fourier analysis on the Boolean cube
people.bio: O'Donnell developed and systematized analytic methods for Boolean functions. With Mossel and Oleszkiewicz he proved an invariance principle and the Majority Is Stablest theorem.
people.impact: Fourier coefficients encode how a function depends on its coordinates. Noise stability and influence connect these coefficients to learning, PCPs and approximation.

sections.title: The Fourier basis is finite
sections.text: The characters χS(x)=∏ᵢ∈Sxᵢ form an orthonormal basis under the uniform measure on {−1,1}ⁿ. Every real-valued function on the cube has a unique expansion.

sections.title: Noise reveals spectral structure
sections.text: If each coordinate pair has correlation ρ, noise stability is ΣSρ^{|S|}f̂(S)². High-degree components are damped when |ρ|<1. For Boolean-valued f, coordinate influence is ΣS∋ᵢf̂(S)².

sections.title: Why majority enters
sections.text: For fixed positive noise correlation, balanced Boolean functions with sufficiently small coordinate influences have stability at most the asymptotic majority value plus a small error. The Mossel–O’Donnell–Oleszkiewicz invariance principle transfers the problem toward Gaussian space.

people.name: Michel Goemans
people.title: Round geometry into a cut
people.bio: Goemans and Williamson developed the celebrated semidefinite-programming approximation algorithm for MAX-CUT. It turns a vector solution into a cut by a random hyperplane.
people.impact: The separation probability of vectors at angle θ is θ/π. Comparing this with their SDP contribution yields the approximation guarantee.

sections.title: Replace signs by vectors
sections.text: A cut assigns each vertex a sign xᵢ. Its objective is Σwᵢⱼ(1−xᵢxⱼ)/2 for nonnegative edge weights. Replacing signs by unit vectors relaxes the discrete problem to an SDP.

sections.title: Round with a random hyperplane
sections.text: Choose a rotationally symmetric Gaussian vector g and use the sign of ⟨g,vᵢ⟩. Two vectors at angle θ are separated with probability θ/π. Compare this with their SDP contribution (1−cosθ)/2.

sections.title: The guarantee and its boundary
sections.text: The expected cut value is at least αGW times the SDP value and hence at least αGW times the true optimum, up to numerical precision. UGC-based hardness gives a matching threshold, but that optimality statement is conditional.

people.name: Prasad Raghavendra
people.title: A unified theory of CSP approximation
people.bio: Raghavendra proved that a canonical SDP framework gives optimal approximation guarantees for finite constraint languages, conditional on the Unique Games Conjecture.
people.formula: UGC ⇒ optimality of the basic SDP framework
people.impact: The theorem concerns fixed finite-domain, bounded-arity maximum CSPs and asymptotic approximation guarantees. It is not a claim that SDP solves every optimization problem exactly.

sections.title: A fixed constraint language
sections.text: Fix a finite domain and a finite set of bounded-arity predicates. The task is to maximize the fraction or weight of satisfied constraints. This framework includes many, but not all, optimization problems.

sections.title: Local distributions and vectors
sections.text: The basic SDP combines vector correlations with local distributions on constraint scopes. Pairwise inner products alone do not describe arbitrary higher-arity constraints. A genuine assignment gives a feasible solution, while an SDP solution may not correspond to any global assignment.

sections.title: A conditional classification
sections.text: Raghavendra connects the achievable rounding guarantees to matching Unique-Games-based hardness, with arbitrarily small slack. The theorem turns a problem-by-problem approximation search into a unified framework, though finding a simple closed-form threshold may still be difficult.
sections.math: UGC + SDP integrality gap → optimal approximation boundary

people.name: Jean-Bernard Lasserre
people.title: Optimization through moments
people.bio: Lasserre developed a hierarchy of semidefinite relaxations for polynomial optimization. Moments and sums of squares connect algorithms with algebraic certificates.
people.impact: A low-degree pseudoexpectation satisfies selected consistency and positivity conditions without necessarily coming from a real distribution. Higher levels impose stronger conditions at greater cost.

sections.title: Replace an assignment by moments
sections.text: A distribution on Boolean assignments determines moments of every monomial. A relaxation retains moments only through degree 2d, expressed as a linear functional Ẽ. It must normalize 1 and annihilate the equality constraints at allowed degrees.

sections.title: Positivity becomes an SDP
sections.text: For monomials xᵅ of degree at most d, form Mᵅᵝ=Ẽ[xᵅ⁺ᵝ]. Requiring Ẽ[p²]≥0 for every degree-d polynomial p is equivalent to M being positive semidefinite.

sections.title: A hierarchy, not a miracle
sections.text: As the level rises, feasible truncated moment sets become more restricted, and maximization upper bounds decrease. For Boolean problems, sufficiently high levels are exact. Fixed levels have SDP size n^{O(d)}, with numerical precision conditions still relevant.

sections.title: The proof side
sections.text: The dual seeks bounded-degree sum-of-squares certificates modulo the constraints. General polynomial optimization needs appropriate compactness or positivity assumptions for convergence claims. A pseudoexpectation obstructs a low-degree certificate without necessarily describing a real probability measure.
sections.math: pseudoexpectation ↔ obstruction to a low-degree refutation

sources.label: Global Optimization with Polynomials and the Problem of Moments

questions: Can you build the degree-two moment matrix for three variables?
How does a pseudoexpectation certify a proof-system lower bound?
Which additional moment constraints first detect an inconsistent cycle?

people.name: Boris Weisfeiler
people.title: Refining the information in a graph
people.bio: Weisfeiler worked in algebra and group theory. With Andrei Leman, he developed graph-refinement ideas that became central to isomorphism, finite model theory and later machine-learning expressiveness.
people.impact: Vertex color refinement is an isomorphism invariant, not a complete test. Equally sized regular graphs already show that local aggregation can miss global differences.

sections.title: Refine without guessing labels
sections.text: The vertex update records a vertex’s old color and the multiset of its neighbors’ colors. Assign equal new colors exactly when these records agree. Run comparison with a common encoding, not unrelated color names in each graph.

sections.title: Why one dimension fails
sections.text: Starting from one color, every vertex of a d-regular graph sees the same multiset forever. Two nonisomorphic d-regular graphs of equal order are therefore indistinguishable by this basic procedure. Rigidity and automorphism count are separate issues.
sections.math: same regular degree + same order ⇒ same 1-WL histogram

sections.title: Tuples, logic and limitations
sections.text: Higher-dimensional versions refine tuples. Precise correspondences with counting logic depend on conventions and indexing. Cai–Fürer–Immerman constructions give nonisomorphic graph families requiring linearly many variables to distinguish, exposing a global parity obstruction.

sources.label: A Lower Bound on the Number of Variables in First Order Logic

questions: Can you exhibit two connected regular graphs that 1-WL cannot distinguish?
What global parity does a CFI gadget encode?
How does a pebble game represent bounded-variable logic?

people.name: Neil Immerman
people.title: Computation described by logic
people.bio: Immerman helped establish descriptive complexity and independently proved closure of nondeterministic space under complement. His work connects machines, logical languages and graph algorithms.
people.impact: Inductive counting can certify non-reachability in logarithmic space. On ordered finite structures, fixed-point logic also captures polynomial-time computation.

sections.title: Nondeterminism certifies absence
sections.text: Directed reachability is NL-complete. Immerman and Szelepcsényi independently proved that its complement is in NL. The method tracks the number of vertices reachable within k steps rather than storing all of them.

sections.title: Why a count makes the certificate trustworthy
sections.text: Given the correct number of reachable vertices, a nondeterministic computation can enumerate witnessed reachable vertices and reject if the count is wrong. This supports an inductive update of the next reachable-set size using logarithmic workspace.

sections.title: Logic captures a resource bound
sections.text: On finite structures equipped with a linear order, first-order logic with transitive closure captures NL, and least fixed-point logic captures P. The order hypothesis in the Immerman–Vardi theorem is essential to its stated form.
sections.math: FO(LFP) = P on ordered finite structures

sources.label: Nondeterministic Space is Closed Under Complementation

questions: How can an exact count certify that no reachable vertex was omitted?
Where does the order enter the characterization of P?

people.name: Haim Gaifman
people.title: The locality of first-order logic
people.bio: Gaifman proved a normal-form theorem expressing first-order sentences through local properties and separated witnesses. It became foundational in finite model theory.
people.impact: Bounded logical depth limits the scale of local inspection. It does not mean that first-order truth is determined solely by frequencies seen from a random vertex.

sections.title: The normal form
sections.text: Every first-order sentence over a finite relational vocabulary is equivalent to a Boolean combination of basic local sentences. Such a sentence asks for finitely many sufficiently separated vertices, all satisfying a specified local formula.

sections.title: Locality is not frequency alone
sections.text: For bounded-degree graph sequences, Benjamini–Schramm convergence records the probabilities of rooted neighborhoods. A rare feature can occur at one vertex and disappear from those probabilities, while an existential FO sentence still detects it.

sections.title: Why algorithms need more than a radius
sections.text: A fixed-radius ball can still be huge when degrees are unbounded. Algorithmic applications therefore combine locality with structural sparsity or other restrictions. Locality does not make arbitrary-graph model checking automatically easy.
sections.math: logical locality + structural control → algorithmic leverage

sources.label: On Local and Non-Local Properties · original chapter

questions: Can one exceptional vertex change FO truth without changing a local limit?
What do separated witnesses add to purely local formulas?
Why does a sparse neighborhood need not have bounded size?

people.name: Jaroslav Nešetřil
people.title: Sparsity with structural meaning
people.bio: Nešetřil shaped graph homomorphism theory, Ramsey theory and structural sparsity. With Ossona de Mendez he developed bounded-expansion and nowhere-dense classes.
people.impact: For bounded expansion, this bound applies to every depth-r shallow minor H. Sparse structure remains sparse after bounded-radius contractions.

sections.title: Few edges is not enough
sections.text: Subdividing every edge of a clique once gives a graph of bounded average degree, but depth-one contractions recover the original clique. A useful sparsity notion must control what is revealed by local contraction.
sections.math: subdivide Kₙ → sparse graph → shallow minor Kₙ

sections.title: Bounded expansion and nowhere density
sections.text: Bounded expansion bounds the density of every fixed-depth shallow minor by a function of that depth. Nowhere density instead excludes sufficiently large clique shallow minors at each fixed depth. It is a weaker structural restriction.
sections.math: ∀r ∃N(r): K_N(r) is not a depth-r shallow minor

sections.title: Logic, algorithms and homomorphisms
sections.text: Nešetřil and Ossona de Mendez developed the structural framework underlying important model-checking results. Dvořák–Král’–Thomas obtained linear-time FO model checking for bounded expansion, and Grohe–Kreutzer–Siebertz almost-linear algorithms for effectively nowhere-dense classes. Nešetřil’s work with Hell also made graph homomorphisms central to coloring and CSPs.

sources.label: Characterisations and Examples of Graph Classes with Bounded Expansion

questions: Can you construct the shallow minor that recovers a subdivided clique?
